The standard mitigation would be for the application to register and identify the user using a combination of the IdP ID (serving as a namespace) and the user's ID in the IdP.
reviewSteps: Verify that, if the application supports multiple identity providers (IdPs), the user's identity cannot be spoofed via another supported identity provider (eg. by using the same user identifier). The standard mitigation would be for the application to register and identify the user using a combination of the IdP ID (serving as a namespace) and the user's ID in the IdP.

asvs.name: V6.8.2 Authentication with an Identity Provider
asvs.description: Verify that the presence and integrity of digital signatures on authentication assertions (for example on JWTs or SAML assertions) are always validated, rejecting any assertions that are unsigned or have invalid signatures.
reviewSteps: Verify that the presence and integrity of digital signatures on authentication assertions (for example on JWTs or SAML assertions) are always validated, rejecting any assertions that are unsigned or have invalid signatures.

asvs.name: V6.8.3 Authentication with an Identity Provider
asvs.description: Verify that SAML assertions are uniquely processed and used only once within the validity period to prevent replay attacks.
reviewSteps: Verify that SAML assertions are uniquely processed and used only once within the validity period to prevent replay attacks.

asvs.name: V6.8.4 Authentication with an Identity Provider
asvs.description: Verify that, if an application uses a separate Identity Provider (IdP) and expects specific authentication strength, methods, or recentness for specific functions, the application verifies this using the information returned by the IdP. For example, if OIDC is used, this might be achieved by validating ID Token claims such as 'acr', 'amr', and 'authtime' (if present). If the IdP does not provide this information, the application must have a documented fallback approach that assumes that the minimum strength authentication mechanism was used (for example, single-factor authentication using username and password).
reviewSteps: Verify that, if an application uses a separate Identity Provider (IdP) and expects specific authentication strength, methods, or recentness for specific functions, the application verifies this using the information returned by the IdP. For example, if OIDC is used, this might be achieved by validating ID Token claims such as 'acr', 'amr', and 'authtime' (if present). If the IdP does not provide this information, the application must have a documented fallback approach that assumes that the minimum strength authentication mechanism was used (for example, single-factor authentication using username and password).

asvs.name: V7.1.1 Session Management Documentation
asvs.description: Verify that the user's session inactivity timeout and absolute maximum session lifetime are documented, are appropriate in combination with other controls, and that the documentation includes justification for any deviations from NIST SP 800-63B re-authentication requirements.
reviewSteps: Verify that the user's session inactivity timeout and absolute maximum session lifetime are documented, are appropriate in combination with other controls, and that the documentation includes justification for any deviations from NIST SP 800-63B re-authentication requirements.

asvs.name: V7.1.2 Session Management Documentation
asvs.description: Verify that the documentation defines how many concurrent (parallel) sessions are allowed for one account as well as the intended behaviors and actions to be taken when the maximum number of active sessions is reached.
reviewSteps: Verify that the documentation defines how many concurrent (parallel) sessions are allowed for one account as well as the intended behaviors and actions to be taken when the maximum number of active sessions is reached.

asvs.name: V7.1.3 Session Management Documentation
asvs.description: Verify that all systems that create and manage user sessions as part of a federated identity management ecosystem (such as SSO systems) are documented along with controls to coordinate session lifetimes, termination, and any other conditions that require re-authentication.
reviewSteps: Verify that all systems that create and manage user sessions as part of a federated identity management ecosystem (such as SSO systems) are documented along with controls to coordinate session lifetimes, termination, and any other conditions that require re-authentication.

asvs.name: V7.2.1 Fundamental Session Management Security
asvs.description: Verify that the application performs all session token verification using a trusted, backend service.
reviewSteps: Verify that the application performs all session token verification using a trusted, backend service.

asvs.name: V7.2.2 Fundamental Session Management Security
asvs.description: Verify that the application uses either self-contained or reference tokens that are dynamically generated for session management, i.e. not using static API secrets and keys.
reviewSteps: Verify that the application uses either self-contained or reference tokens that are dynamically generated for session management, i.e. not using static API secrets and keys.

asvs.name: V7.2.3 Fundamental Session Management Security
asvs.description: Verify that if reference tokens are used to represent user sessions, they are unique and generated using a cryptographically secure pseudo-random number generator (CSPRNG) and possess at least 128 bits of entropy.
reviewSteps: Verify that if reference tokens are used to represent user sessions, they are unique and generated using a cryptographically secure pseudo-random number generator (CSPRNG) and possess at least 128 bits of entropy.

asvs.name: V7.2.4 Fundamental Session Management Security
asvs.description: Verify that the application generates a new session token on user authentication, including re-authentication, and terminates the current session token.
reviewSteps: Verify that the application generates a new session token on user authentication, including re-authentication, and terminates the current session token.

asvs.name: V7.3.1 Session Timeout
asvs.description: Verify that there is an inactivity timeout such that re-authentication is enforced according to risk analysis and documented security decisions.
reviewSteps: Verify that there is an inactivity timeout such that re-authentication is enforced according to risk analysis and documented security decisions.

asvs.name: V7.3.2 Session Timeout
asvs.description: Verify that there is an absolute maximum session lifetime such that re-authentication is enforced according to risk analysis and documented security decisions.
reviewSteps: Verify that there is an absolute maximum session lifetime such that re-authentication is enforced according to risk analysis and documented security decisions.

asvs.name: V7.4.1 Session Termination
asvs.description: Verify that when session termination is triggered (such as logout or expiration), the application disallows any further use of the session. For reference tokens or stateful sessions, this means invalidating the session data at the application backend. Applications using self-contained tokens will need a solution such as maintaining a list of terminated tokens, disallowing tokens produced before a per-user date and time or rotating a per-user signing key.
reviewSteps: Verify that when session termination is triggered (such as logout or expiration), the application disallows any further use of the session. For reference tokens or stateful sessions, this means invalidating the session data at the application backend. Applications using self-contained tokens will need a solution such as maintaining a list of terminated tokens, disallowing tokens produced before a per-user date and time or rotating a per-user signing key.

asvs.name: V7.4.2 Session Termination
asvs.description: Verify that the application terminates all active sessions when a user account is disabled or deleted (such as an employee leaving the company).
reviewSteps: Verify that the application terminates all active sessions when a user account is disabled or deleted (such as an employee leaving the company).

asvs.name: V7.4.3 Session Termination
asvs.description: Verify that the application gives the option to terminate all other active sessions after a successful change or removal of any authentication factor (including password change via reset or recovery and, if present, an MFA settings update).
reviewSteps: Verify that the application gives the option to terminate all other active sessions after a successful change or removal of any authentication factor (including password change via reset or recovery and, if present, an MFA settings update).

asvs.name: V7.4.4 Session Termination
asvs.description: Verify that all pages that require authentication have easy and visible access to logout functionality.
reviewSteps: Verify that all pages that require authentication have easy and visible access to logout functionality.

asvs.name: V7.4.5 Session Termination
asvs.description: Verify that application administrators are able to terminate active sessions for an individual user or for all users.
reviewSteps: Verify that application administrators are able to terminate active sessions for an individual user or for all users.

asvs.name: V7.5.1 Defenses Against Session Abuse
asvs.description: Verify that the application requires full re-authentication before allowing modifications to sensitive account attributes which may affect authentication such as email address, phone number, MFA configuration, or other information used in account recovery.
reviewSteps: Verify that the application requires full re-authentication before allowing modifications to sensitive account attributes which may affect authentication such as email address, phone number, MFA configuration, or other information used in account recovery.

asvs.name: V7.5.2 Defenses Against Session Abuse
asvs.description: Verify that users are able to view and (having authenticated again with at least one factor) terminate any or all currently active sessions.
reviewSteps: Verify that users are able to view and (having authenticated again with at least one factor) terminate any or all currently active sessions.

asvs.name: V7.5.3 Defenses Against Session Abuse
asvs.description: Verify that the application requires further authentication with at least one factor or secondary verification before performing highly sensitive transactions or operations.
reviewSteps: Verify that the application requires further authentication with at least one factor or secondary verification before performing highly sensitive transactions or operations.

asvs.name: V7.6.1 Federated Re-authentication
asvs.description: Verify that session lifetime and termination between Relying Parties (RPs) and Identity Providers (IdPs) behave as documented, requiring re-authentication as necessary such as when the maximum time between IdP authentication events is reached.
reviewSteps: Verify that session lifetime and termination between Relying Parties (RPs) and Identity Providers (IdPs) behave as documented, requiring re-authentication as necessary such as when the maximum time between IdP authentication events is reached.

asvs.name: V7.6.2 Federated Re-authentication
asvs.description: Verify that creation of a session requires either the user's consent or an explicit action, preventing the creation of new application sessions without user interaction.
reviewSteps: Verify that creation of a session requires either the user's consent or an explicit action, preventing the creation of new application sessions without user interaction.

asvs.name: V8.1.1 Authorization Documentation
asvs.description: Verify that authorization documentation defines rules for restricting function-level and data-specific access based on consumer permissions and resource attributes.
reviewSteps: Verify that authorization documentation defines rules for restricting function-level and data-specific access based on consumer permissions and resource attributes.

asvs.name: V8.1.2 Authorization Documentation
asvs.description: Verify that authorization documentation defines rules for field-level access restrictions (both read and write) based on consumer permissions and resource attributes. Note that these rules might depend on other attribute values of the relevant data object, such as state or status.
reviewSteps: Verify that authorization documentation defines rules for field-level access restrictions (both read and write) based on consumer permissions and resource attributes. Note that these rules might depend on other attribute values of the relevant data object, such as state or status.

asvs.name: V8.1.3 Authorization Documentation
asvs.description: Verify that the application's documentation defines the environmental and contextual attributes (including but not limited to, time of day, user location, IP address, or device) that are used in the application to make security decisions, including those pertaining to authentication and authorization.
reviewSteps: Verify that the application's documentation defines the environmental and contextual attributes (including but not limited to, time of day, user location, IP address, or device) that are used in the application to make security decisions, including those pertaining to authentication and authorization.

asvs.name: V8.1.4 Authorization Documentation
asvs.description: Verify that authentication and authorization documentation defines how environmental and contextual factors are used in decision-making, in addition to function-level, data-specific, and field-level authorization. This should include the attributes evaluated, thresholds for risk, and actions taken (e.g., allow, challenge, deny, step-up authentication).
reviewSteps: Verify that authentication and authorization documentation defines how environmental and contextual factors are used in decision-making, in addition to function-level, data-specific, and field-level authorization. This should include the attributes evaluated, thresholds for risk, and actions taken (e.g., allow, challenge, deny, step-up authentication).

asvs.name: V8.2.1 General Authorization Design
asvs.description: Verify that the application ensures that function-level access is restricted to consumers with explicit permissions.
reviewSteps: Verify that the application ensures that function-level access is restricted to consumers with explicit permissions.

asvs.name: V8.2.2 General Authorization Design
asvs.description: Verify that the application ensures that data-specific access is restricted to consumers with explicit permissions to specific data items to mitigate insecure direct object reference (IDOR) and broken object level authorization (BOLA).
reviewSteps: Verify that the application ensures that data-specific access is restricted to consumers with explicit permissions to specific data items to mitigate insecure direct object reference (IDOR) and broken object level authorization (BOLA).

asvs.name: V8.2.3 General Authorization Design
asvs.description: Verify that the application ensures that field-level access is restricted to consumers with explicit permissions to specific fields to mitigate broken object property level authorization (BOPLA).
reviewSteps: Verify that the application ensures that field-level access is restricted to consumers with explicit permissions to specific fields to mitigate broken object property level authorization (BOPLA).

asvs.name: V8.2.4 General Authorization Design
asvs.description: Verify that adaptive security controls based on a consumer's environmental and contextual attributes (such as time of day, location, IP address, or device) are implemented for authentication and authorization decisions, as defined in the application's documentation. These controls must be applied when the consumer tries to start a new session and also during an existing session.
reviewSteps: Verify that adaptive security controls based on a consumer's environmental and contextual attributes (such as time of day, location, IP address, or device) are implemented for authentication and authorization decisions, as defined in the application's documentation. These controls must be applied when the consumer tries to start a new session and also during an existing session.

asvs.name: V8.3.1 Operation Level Authorization
asvs.description: Verify that the application enforces authorization rules at a trusted service layer and doesn't rely on controls that an untrusted consumer could manipulate, such as client-side JavaScript.
reviewSteps: Verify that the application enforces authorization rules at a trusted service layer and doesn't rely on controls that an untrusted consumer could manipulate, such as client-side JavaScript.

asvs.name: V8.3.2 Operation Level Authorization
asvs.description: Verify that changes to values on which authorization decisions are made are applied immediately. Where changes cannot be applied immediately, (such as when relying on data in self-contained tokens), there must be mitigating controls to alert when a consumer performs an action when they are no longer authorized to do so and revert the change. Note that this alternative would not mitigate information leakage.
reviewSteps: Verify that changes to values on which authorization decisions are made are applied immediately. Where changes cannot be applied immediately, (such as when relying on data in self-contained tokens), there must be mitigating controls to alert when a consumer performs an action when they are no longer authorized to do so and revert the change. Note that this alternative would not mitigate information leakage.

asvs.name: V8.3.3 Operation Level Authorization
asvs.description: Verify that access to an object is based on the originating subject's (e.g. consumer's) permissions, not on the permissions of any intermediary or service acting on their behalf. For example, if a consumer calls a web service using a self-contained token for authentication, and the service then requests data from a different service, the second service will use the consumer's token, rather than a machine-to-machine token from the first service, to make permission decisions.
reviewSteps: Verify that access to an object is based on the originating subject's (e.g. consumer's) permissions, not on the permissions of any intermediary or service acting on their behalf. For example, if a consumer calls a web service using a self-contained token for authentication, and the service then requests data from a different service, the second service will use the consumer's token, rather than a machine-to-machine token from the first service, to make permission decisions.

asvs.name: V8.4.1 Other Authorization Considerations
asvs.description: Verify that multi-tenant applications use cross-tenant controls to ensure consumer operations will never affect tenants with which they do not have permissions to interact.
reviewSteps: Verify that multi-tenant applications use cross-tenant controls to ensure consumer operations will never affect tenants with which they do not have permissions to interact.

asvs.name: V8.4.2 Other Authorization Considerations
asvs.description: Verify that access to administrative interfaces incorporates multiple layers of security, including continuous consumer identity verification, device security posture assessment, and contextual risk analysis, ensuring that network location or trusted endpoints are not the sole factors for authorization even though they may reduce the likelihood of unauthorized access.
reviewSteps: Verify that access to administrative interfaces incorporates multiple layers of security, including continuous consumer identity verification, device security posture assessment, and contextual risk analysis, ensuring that network location or trusted endpoints are not the sole factors for authorization even though they may reduce the likelihood of unauthorized access.

asvs.name: V9.1.1 Token source and integrity
asvs.description: Verify that self-contained tokens are validated using their digital signature or MAC to protect against tampering before accepting the token's contents.
reviewSteps: Verify that self-contained tokens are validated using their digital signature or MAC to protect against tampering before accepting the token's contents.

asvs.name: V9.1.2 Token source and integrity
asvs.description: Verify that only algorithms on an allowlist can be used to create and verify self-contained tokens, for a given context. The allowlist must include the permitted algorithms, ideally only either symmetric or asymmetric algorithms, and must not include the 'None' algorithm. If both symmetric and asymmetric must be supported, additional controls will be needed to prevent key confusion.
reviewSteps: Verify that only algorithms on an allowlist can be used to create and verify self-contained tokens, for a given context. The allowlist must include the permitted algorithms, ideally only either symmetric or asymmetric algorithms, and must not include the 'None' algorithm. If both symmetric and asymmetric must be supported, additional controls will be needed to prevent key confusion.

asvs.name: V9.1.3 Token source and integrity
asvs.description: Verify that key material that is used to validate self-contained tokens is from trusted pre-configured sources for the token issuer, preventing attackers from specifying untrusted sources and keys. For JWTs and other JWS structures, headers such as 'jku', 'x5u', and 'jwk' must be validated against an allowlist of trusted sources.
reviewSteps: Verify that key material that is used to validate self-contained tokens is from trusted pre-configured sources for the token issuer, preventing attackers from specifying untrusted sources and keys. For JWTs and other JWS structures, headers such as 'jku', 'x5u', and 'jwk' must be validated against an allowlist of trusted sources.

asvs.name: V9.2.1 Token content
asvs.description: Verify that, if a validity time span is present in the token data, the token and its content are accepted only if the verification time is within this validity time span. For example, for JWTs, the claims 'nbf' and 'exp' must be verified.
reviewSteps: Verify that, if a validity time span is present in the token data, the token and its content are accepted only if the verification time is within this validity time span. For example, for JWTs, the claims 'nbf' and 'exp' must be verified.

asvs.name: V9.2.2 Token content
asvs.description: Verify that the service receiving a token validates the token to be the correct type and is meant for the intended purpose before accepting the token's contents. For example, only access tokens can be accepted for authorization decisions and only ID Tokens can be used for proving user authentication.
reviewSteps: Verify that the service receiving a token validates the token to be the correct type and is meant for the intended purpose before accepting the token's contents. For example, only access tokens can be accepted for authorization decisions and only ID Tokens can be used for proving user authentication.

asvs.name: V9.2.3 Token content
asvs.description: Verify that the service only accepts tokens which are intended for use with that service (audience). For JWTs, this can be achieved by validating the 'aud' claim against an allowlist defined in the service.
reviewSteps: Verify that the service only accepts tokens which are intended for use with that service (audience). For JWTs, this can be achieved by validating the 'aud' claim against an allowlist defined in the service.

asvs.name: V9.2.4 Token content
asvs.description: Verify that, if a token issuer uses the same private key for issuing tokens to different audiences, the issued tokens contain an audience restriction that uniquely identifies the intended audiences. This will prevent a token from being reused with an unintended audience. If the audience identifier is dynamically provisioned, the token issuer must validate these audiences in order to make sure that they do not result in audience impersonation.
reviewSteps: Verify that, if a token issuer uses the same private key for issuing tokens to different audiences, the issued tokens contain an audience restriction that uniquely identifies the intended audiences. This will prevent a token from being reused with an unintended audience. If the audience identifier is dynamically provisioned, the token issuer must validate these audiences in order to make sure that they do not result in audience impersonation.

asvs.name: V10.1.1 Generic OAuth and OIDC Security
asvs.description: Verify that tokens are only sent to components that strictly need them. For example, when using a backend-for-frontend pattern for browser-based JavaScript applications, access and refresh tokens shall only be accessible for the backend.
reviewSteps: Verify that tokens are only sent to components that strictly need them. For example, when using a backend-for-frontend pattern for browser-based JavaScript applications, access and refresh tokens shall only be accessible for the backend.

asvs.name: V10.1.2 Generic OAuth and OIDC Security
asvs.description: Verify that the client only accepts values from the authorization server (such as the authorization code or ID Token) if these values result from an authorization flow that was initiated by the same user agent session and transaction. This requires that client-generated secrets, such as the proof key for code exchange (PKCE) 'codeverifier', 'state' or OIDC 'nonce', are not guessable, are specific to the transaction, and are securely bound to both the client and the user agent session in which the transaction was started.
reviewSteps: Verify that the client only accepts values from the authorization server (such as the authorization code or ID Token) if these values result from an authorization flow that was initiated by the same user agent session and transaction. This requires that client-generated secrets, such as the proof key for code exchange (PKCE) 'codeverifier', 'state' or OIDC 'nonce', are not guessable, are specific to the transaction, and are securely bound to both the client and the user agent session in which the transaction was started.

asvs.name: V10.2.1 OAuth Client
asvs.description: Verify that, if the code flow is used, the OAuth client has protection against browser-based request forgery attacks, commonly known as cross-site request forgery (CSRF), which trigger token requests, either by using proof key for code exchange (PKCE) functionality or checking the 'state' parameter that was sent in the authorization request.
reviewSteps: Verify that, if the code flow is used, the OAuth client has protection against browser-based request forgery attacks, commonly known as cross-site request forgery (CSRF), which trigger token requests, either by using proof key for code exchange (PKCE) functionality or checking the 'state' parameter that was sent in the authorization request.

asvs.name: V10.2.2 OAuth Client
asvs.description: Verify that, if the OAuth client can interact with more than one authorization server, it has a defense against mix-up attacks. For example, it could require that the authorization server return the 'iss' parameter value and validate it in the authorization response and the token response.
reviewSteps: Verify that, if the OAuth client can interact with more than one authorization server, it has a defense against mix-up attacks. For example, it could require that the authorization server return the 'iss' parameter value and validate it in the authorization response and the token response.

asvs.name: V10.2.3 OAuth Client
asvs.description: Verify that the OAuth client only requests the required scopes (or other authorization parameters) in requests to the authorization server.
reviewSteps: Verify that the OAuth client only requests the required scopes (or other authorization parameters) in requests to the authorization server.

asvs.name: V10.3.1 OAuth Resource Server
asvs.description: Verify that the resource server only accepts access tokens that are intended for use with that service (audience). The audience may be included in a structured access token (such as the 'aud' claim in JWT), or it can be checked using the token introspection endpoint.
reviewSteps: Verify that the resource server only accepts access tokens that are intended for use with that service (audience). The audience may be included in a structured access token (such as the 'aud' claim in JWT), or it can be checked using the token introspection endpoint.

asvs.name: V10.3.2 OAuth Resource Server
asvs.description: Verify that the resource server enforces authorization decisions based on claims from the access token that define delegated authorization. If claims such as 'sub', 'scope', and 'authorizationdetails' are present, they must be part of the decision.
reviewSteps: Verify that the resource server enforces authorization decisions based on claims from the access token that define delegated authorization. If claims such as 'sub', 'scope', and 'authorizationdetails' are present, they must be part of the decision.

asvs.name: V10.3.3 OAuth Resource Server
asvs.description: Verify that if an access control decision requires identifying a unique user from an access token (JWT or related token introspection response), the resource server identifies the user from claims that cannot be reassigned to other users. Typically, it means using a combination of 'iss' and 'sub' claims.
reviewSteps: Verify that if an access control decision requires identifying a unique user from an access token (JWT or related token introspection response), the resource server identifies the user from claims that cannot be reassigned to other users. Typically, it means using a combination of 'iss' and 'sub' claims.

asvs.name: V10.3.4 OAuth Resource Server
asvs.description: Verify that, if the resource server requires specific authentication strength, methods, or recentness, it verifies that the presented access token satisfies these constraints. For example, if present, using the OIDC 'acr', 'amr' and 'authtime' claims respectively.
reviewSteps: Verify that, if the resource server requires specific authentication strength, methods, or recentness, it verifies that the presented access token satisfies these constraints. For example, if present, using the OIDC 'acr', 'amr' and 'authtime' claims respectively.

asvs.name: V10.3.5 OAuth Resource Server
asvs.description: Verify that the resource server prevents the use of stolen access tokens or replay of access tokens (from unauthorized parties) by requiring sender-constrained access tokens, either Mutual TLS for OAuth 2 or OAuth 2 Demonstration of Proof of Possession (DPoP).
reviewSteps: Verify that the resource server prevents the use of stolen access tokens or replay of access tokens (from unauthorized parties) by requiring sender-constrained access tokens, either Mutual TLS for OAuth 2 or OAuth 2 Demonstration of Proof of Possession (DPoP).

asvs.name: V10.4.1 OAuth Authorization Server
asvs.description: Verify that the authorization server validates redirect URIs based on a client-specific allowlist of pre-registered URIs using exact string comparison.
reviewSteps: Verify that the authorization server validates redirect URIs based on a client-specific allowlist of pre-registered URIs using exact string comparison.

asvs.name: V10.4.2 OAuth Authorization Server
asvs.description: Verify that, if the authorization server returns the authorization code in the authorization response, it can be used only once for a token request. For the second valid request with an authorization code that has already been used to issue an access token, the authorization server must reject a token request and revoke any issued tokens related to the authorization code.
reviewSteps: Verify that, if the authorization server returns the authorization code in the authorization response, it can be used only once for a token request. For the second valid request with an authorization code that has already been used to issue an access token, the authorization server must reject a token request and revoke any issued tokens related to the authorization code.

asvs.name: V10.4.3 OAuth Authorization Server
asvs.description: Verify that the authorization code is short-lived. The maximum lifetime can be up to 10 minutes for L1 and L2 applications and up to 1 minute for L3 applications.
reviewSteps: Verify that the authorization code is short-lived. The maximum lifetime can be up to 10 minutes for L1 and L2 applications and up to 1 minute for L3 applications.

asvs.name: V10.4.4 OAuth Authorization Server
asvs.description: Verify that for a given client, the authorization server only allows the usage of grants that this client needs to use. Note that the grants 'token' (Implicit flow) and 'password' (Resource Owner Password Credentials flow) must no longer be used.
reviewSteps: Verify that for a given client, the authorization server only allows the usage of grants that this client needs to use. Note that the grants 'token' (Implicit flow) and 'password' (Resource Owner Password Credentials flow) must no longer be used.

asvs.name: V10.4.5 OAuth Authorization Server
asvs.description: Verify that the authorization server mitigates refresh token replay attacks for public clients, preferably using sender-constrained refresh tokens, i.e., Demonstrating Proof of Possession (DPoP) or Certificate-Bound Access Tokens using mutual TLS (mTLS). For L1 and L2 applications, refresh token rotation may be used. If refresh token rotation is used, the authorization server must invalidate the refresh token after usage, and revoke all refresh tokens for that authorization if an already used and invalidated refresh token is provided.
reviewSteps: Verify that the authorization server mitigates refresh token replay attacks for public clients, preferably using sender-constrained refresh tokens, i.e., Demonstrating Proof of Possession (DPoP) or Certificate-Bound Access Tokens using mutual TLS (mTLS). For L1 and L2 applications, refresh token rotation may be used. If refresh token rotation is used, the authorization server must invalidate the refresh token after usage, and revoke all refresh tokens for that authorization if an already used and invalidated refresh token is provided.

asvs.name: V10.4.6 OAuth Authorization Server
asvs.description: Verify that, if the code grant is used, the authorization server mitigates authorization code interception attacks by requiring proof key for code exchange (PKCE). For authorization requests, the authorization server must require a valid 'codechallenge' value and must not accept a 'codechallengemethod' value of 'plain'. For a token request, it must require validation of the 'codeverifier' parameter.
reviewSteps: Verify that, if the code grant is used, the authorization server mitigates authorization code interception attacks by requiring proof key for code exchange (PKCE). For authorization requests, the authorization server must require a valid 'codechallenge' value and must not accept a 'codechallengemethod' value of 'plain'. For a token request, it must require validation of the 'codeverifier' parameter.

asvs.name: V10.4.7 OAuth Authorization Server
asvs.description: Verify that if the authorization server supports unauthenticated dynamic client registration, it mitigates the risk of malicious client applications. It must validate client metadata such as any registered URIs, ensure the user's consent, and warn the user before processing an authorization request with an untrusted client application.
reviewSteps: Verify that if the authorization server supports unauthenticated dynamic client registration, it mitigates the risk of malicious client applications. It must validate client metadata such as any registered URIs, ensure the user's consent, and warn the user before processing an authorization request with an untrusted client application.

asvs.name: V10.4.8 OAuth Authorization Server
asvs.description: Verify that refresh tokens have an absolute expiration, including if sliding refresh token expiration is applied.
reviewSteps: Verify that refresh tokens have an absolute expiration, including if sliding refresh token expiration is applied.

asvs.name: V10.4.9 OAuth Authorization Server
asvs.description: Verify that refresh tokens and reference access tokens can be revoked by an authorized user using the authorization server user interface, to mitigate the risk of malicious clients or stolen tokens.
reviewSteps: Verify that refresh tokens and reference access tokens can be revoked by an authorized user using the authorization server user interface, to mitigate the risk of malicious clients or stolen tokens.

asvs.name: V10.4.10 OAuth Authorization Server
asvs.description: Verify that confidential client is authenticated for client-to-authorized server backchannel requests such as token requests, pushed authorization requests (PAR), and token revocation requests.
reviewSteps: Verify that confidential client is authenticated for client-to-authorized server backchannel requests such as token requests, pushed authorization requests (PAR), and token revocation requests.

asvs.name: V10.4.11 OAuth Authorization Server
asvs.description: Verify that the authorization server configuration only assigns the required scopes to the OAuth client.
reviewSteps: Verify that the authorization server configuration only assigns the required scopes to the OAuth client.

asvs.name: V10.4.12 OAuth Authorization Server
asvs.description: Verify that for a given client, the authorization server only allows the 'responsemode' value that this client needs to use. For example, by having the authorization server validate this value against the expected values or by using pushed authorization request (PAR) or JWT-secured Authorization Request (JAR).
reviewSteps: Verify that for a given client, the authorization server only allows the 'responsemode' value that this client needs to use. For example, by having the authorization server validate this value against the expected values or by using pushed authorization request (PAR) or JWT-secured Authorization Request (JAR).

asvs.name: V10.4.13 OAuth Authorization Server
asvs.description: Verify that grant type 'code' is always used together with pushed authorization requests (PAR).
reviewSteps: Verify that grant type 'code' is always used together with pushed authorization requests (PAR).

asvs.name: V10.4.14 OAuth Authorization Server
asvs.description: Verify that the authorization server issues only sender-constrained (Proof-of-Possession) access tokens, either with certificate-bound access tokens using mutual TLS (mTLS) or DPoP-bound access tokens (Demonstration of Proof of Possession).
reviewSteps: Verify that the authorization server issues only sender-constrained (Proof-of-Possession) access tokens, either with certificate-bound access tokens using mutual TLS (mTLS) or DPoP-bound access tokens (Demonstration of Proof of Possession).

asvs.name: V10.4.15 OAuth Authorization Server
asvs.description: Verify that, for a server-side client (which is not executed on the end-user device), the authorization server ensures that the 'authorizationdetails' parameter value is from the client backend and that the user has not tampered with it. For example, by requiring the usage of pushed authorization request (PAR) or JWT-secured Authorization Request (JAR).
reviewSteps: Verify that, for a server-side client (which is not executed on the end-user device), the authorization server ensures that the 'authorizationdetails' parameter value is from the client backend and that the user has not tampered with it. For example, by requiring the usage of pushed authorization request (PAR) or JWT-secured Authorization Request (JAR).

asvs.name: V10.4.16 OAuth Authorization Server
asvs.description: Verify that the client is confidential and the authorization server requires the use of strong client authentication methods (based on public-key cryptography and resistant to replay attacks), such as mutual TLS ('tlsclientauth', 'selfsignedtlsclientauth') or private key JWT ('privatekeyjwt').
reviewSteps: Verify that the client is confidential and the authorization server requires the use of strong client authentication methods (based on public-key cryptography and resistant to replay attacks), such as mutual TLS ('tlsclientauth', 'selfsignedtlsclientauth') or private key JWT ('privatekeyjwt').

asvs.name: V10.5.1 OIDC Client
asvs.description: Verify that the client (as the relying party) mitigates ID Token replay attacks. For example, by ensuring that the 'nonce' claim in the ID Token matches the 'nonce' value sent in the authentication request to the OpenID Provider (in OAuth2 refereed to as the authorization request sent to the authorization server).
reviewSteps: Verify that the client (as the relying party) mitigates ID Token replay attacks. For example, by ensuring that the 'nonce' claim in the ID Token matches the 'nonce' value sent in the authentication request to the OpenID Provider (in OAuth2 refereed to as the authorization request sent to the authorization server).

asvs.name: V10.5.2 OIDC Client
asvs.description: Verify that the client uniquely identifies the user from ID Token claims, usually the 'sub' claim, which cannot be reassigned to other users (for the scope of an identity provider).
reviewSteps: Verify that the client uniquely identifies the user from ID Token claims, usually the 'sub' claim, which cannot be reassigned to other users (for the scope of an identity provider).

asvs.name: V10.5.3 OIDC Client
asvs.description: Verify that the client rejects attempts by a malicious authorization server to impersonate another authorization server through authorization server metadata. The client must reject authorization server metadata if the issuer URL in the authorization server metadata does not exactly match the pre-configured issuer URL expected by the client.
reviewSteps: Verify that the client rejects attempts by a malicious authorization server to impersonate another authorization server through authorization server metadata. The client must reject authorization server metadata if the issuer URL in the authorization server metadata does not exactly match the pre-configured issuer URL expected by the client.

asvs.name: V10.5.4 OIDC Client
asvs.description: Verify that the client validates that the ID Token is intended to be used for that client (audience) by checking that the 'aud' claim from the token is equal to the 'clientid' value for the client.
reviewSteps: Verify that the client validates that the ID Token is intended to be used for that client (audience) by checking that the 'aud' claim from the token is equal to the 'clientid' value for the client.

asvs.name: V10.5.5 OIDC Client
asvs.description: Verify that, when using OIDC back-channel logout, the relying party mitigates denial of service through forced logout and cross-JWT confusion in the logout flow. The client must verify that the logout token is correctly typed with a value of 'logout+jwt', contains the 'event' claim with the correct member name, and does not contain a 'nonce' claim. Note that it is also recommended to have a short expiration (e.g., 2 minutes).
reviewSteps: Verify that, when using OIDC back-channel logout, the relying party mitigates denial of service through forced logout and cross-JWT confusion in the logout flow. The client must verify that the logout token is correctly typed with a value of 'logout+jwt', contains the 'event' claim with the correct member name, and does not contain a 'nonce' claim. Note that it is also recommended to have a short expiration (e.g., 2 minutes).

asvs.name: V10.6.1 OpenID Provider
asvs.description: Verify that the OpenID Provider only allows values 'code', 'ciba', 'idtoken', or 'idtoken code' for response mode. Note that 'code' is preferred over 'idtoken code' (the OIDC Hybrid flow), and 'token' (any Implicit flow) must not be used.
reviewSteps: Verify that the OpenID Provider only allows values 'code', 'ciba', 'idtoken', or 'idtoken code' for response mode. Note that 'code' is preferred over 'idtoken code' (the OIDC Hybrid flow), and 'token' (any Implicit flow) must not be used.

asvs.name: V10.6.2 OpenID Provider
asvs.description: Verify that the OpenID Provider mitigates denial of service through forced logout. By obtaining explicit confirmation from the end-user or, if present, validating parameters in the logout request (initiated by the relying party), such as the 'idtokenhint'.
reviewSteps: Verify that the OpenID Provider mitigates denial of service through forced logout. By obtaining explicit confirmation from the end-user or, if present, validating parameters in the logout request (initiated by the relying party), such as the 'idtokenhint'.

asvs.name: V10.7.1 Consent Management
asvs.description: Verify that the authorization server ensures that the user consents to each authorization request. If the identity of the client cannot be assured, the authorization server must always explicitly prompt the user for consent.
reviewSteps: Verify that the authorization server ensures that the user consents to each authorization request. If the identity of the client cannot be assured, the authorization server must always explicitly prompt the user for consent.

asvs.name: V10.7.2 Consent Management
asvs.description: Verify that when the authorization server prompts for user consent, it presents sufficient and clear information about what is being consented to. When applicable, this should include the nature of the requested authorizations (typically based on scope, resource server, Rich Authorization Requests (RAR) authorization details), the identity of the authorized application, and the lifetime of these authorizations.
reviewSteps: Verify that when the authorization server prompts for user consent, it presents sufficient and clear information about what is being consented to. When applicable, this should include the nature of the requested authorizations (typically based on scope, resource server, Rich Authorization Requests (RAR) authorization details), the identity of the authorized application, and the lifetime of these authorizations.

asvs.name: V10.7.3 Consent Management
asvs.description: Verify that the user can review, modify, and revoke consents which the user has granted through the authorization server.
reviewSteps: Verify that the user can review, modify, and revoke consents which the user has granted through the authorization server.

asvs.name: V11.1.1 Cryptographic Inventory and Documentation
asvs.description: Verify that there is a documented policy for management of cryptographic keys and a cryptographic key lifecycle that follows a key management standard such as NIST SP 800-57. This should include ensuring that keys are not overshared (for example, with more than two entities for shared secrets and more than one entity for private keys).
reviewSteps: Verify that there is a documented policy for management of cryptographic keys and a cryptographic key lifecycle that follows a key management standard such as NIST SP 800-57. This should include ensuring that keys are not overshared (for example, with more than two entities for shared secrets and more than one entity for private keys).

asvs.name: V11.1.2 Cryptographic Inventory and Documentation
asvs.description: Verify that a cryptographic inventory is performed, maintained, regularly updated, and includes all cryptographic keys, algorithms, and certificates used by the application. It must also document where keys can and cannot be used in the system, and the types of data that can and cannot be protected using the keys.
reviewSteps: Verify that a cryptographic inventory is performed, maintained, regularly updated, and includes all cryptographic keys, algorithms, and certificates used by the application. It must also document where keys can and cannot be used in the system, and the types of data that can and cannot be protected using the keys.

asvs.name: V11.1.3 Cryptographic Inventory and Documentation
asvs.description: Verify that cryptographic discovery mechanisms are employed to identify all instances of cryptography in the system, including encryption, hashing, and signing operations.
reviewSteps: Verify that cryptographic discovery mechanisms are employed to identify all instances of cryptography in the system, including encryption, hashing, and signing operations.

asvs.name: V11.1.4 Cryptographic Inventory and Documentation
asvs.description: Verify that a cryptographic inventory is maintained. This must include a documented plan that outlines the migration path to new cryptographic standards, such as post-quantum cryptography, in order to react to future threats.
reviewSteps: Verify that a cryptographic inventory is maintained. This must include a documented plan that outlines the migration path to new cryptographic standards, such as post-quantum cryptography, in order to react to future threats.

asvs.name: V11.2.1 Secure Cryptography Implementation
asvs.description: Verify that industry-validated implementations (including libraries and hardware-accelerated implementations) are used for cryptographic operations.
reviewSteps: Verify that industry-validated implementations (including libraries and hardware-accelerated implementations) are used for cryptographic operations.

asvs.name: V11.2.2 Secure Cryptography Implementation
asvs.description: Verify that the application is designed with crypto agility such that random number, authenticated encryption, MAC, or hashing algorithms, key lengths, rounds, ciphers and modes can be reconfigured, upgraded, or swapped at any time, to protect against cryptographic breaks. Similarly, it must also be possible to replace keys and passwords and re-encrypt data. This will allow for seamless upgrades to post-quantum cryptography (PQC), once high-assurance implementations of approved PQC schemes or standards are widely available.
reviewSteps: Verify that the application is designed with crypto agility such that random number, authenticated encryption, MAC, or hashing algorithms, key lengths, rounds, ciphers and modes can be reconfigured, upgraded, or swapped at any time, to protect against cryptographic breaks. Similarly, it must also be possible to replace keys and passwords and re-encrypt data. This will allow for seamless upgrades to post-quantum cryptography (PQC), once high-assurance implementations of approved PQC schemes or standards are widely available.

asvs.name: V11.2.3 Secure Cryptography Implementation
asvs.description: Verify that all cryptographic primitives utilize a minimum of 128-bits of security based on the algorithm, key size, and configuration. For example, a 256-bit ECC key provides roughly 128 bits of security where RSA requires a 3072-bit key to achieve 128 bits of security.
reviewSteps: Verify that all cryptographic primitives utilize a minimum of 128-bits of security based on the algorithm, key size, and configuration. For example, a 256-bit ECC key provides roughly 128 bits of security where RSA requires a 3072-bit key to achieve 128 bits of security.

asvs.name: V11.2.4 Secure Cryptography Implementation
asvs.description: Verify that all cryptographic operations are constant-time, with no 'short-circuit' operations in comparisons, calculations, or returns, to avoid leaking information.
reviewSteps: Verify that all cryptographic operations are constant-time, with no 'short-circuit' operations in comparisons, calculations, or returns, to avoid leaking information.

asvs.name: V11.2.5 Secure Cryptography Implementation
asvs.description: Verify that all cryptographic modules fail securely, and errors are handled in a way that does not enable vulnerabilities, such as Padding Oracle attacks.
reviewSteps: Verify that all cryptographic modules fail securely, and errors are handled in a way that does not enable vulnerabilities, such as Padding Oracle attacks.

asvs.name: V11.3.1 Encryption Algorithms
asvs.description: Verify that insecure block modes (e.g., ECB) and weak padding schemes (e.g., PKCS1 v1.5) are not used.
reviewSteps: Verify that insecure block modes (e.g., ECB) and weak padding schemes (e.g., PKCS1 v1.5) are not used.

asvs.name: V11.3.2 Encryption Algorithms
asvs.description: Verify that only approved ciphers and modes such as AES with GCM are used.
reviewSteps: Verify that only approved ciphers and modes such as AES with GCM are used.

asvs.name: V11.3.3 Encryption Algorithms
asvs.description: Verify that encrypted data is protected against unauthorized modification preferably by using an approved authenticated encryption method or by combining an approved encryption method with an approved MAC algorithm.
reviewSteps: Verify that encrypted data is protected against unauthorized modification preferably by using an approved authenticated encryption method or by combining an approved encryption method with an approved MAC algorithm.

asvs.name: V11.3.4 Encryption Algorithms
asvs.description: Verify that nonces, initialization vectors, and other single-use numbers are not used for more than one encryption key and data-element pair. The method of generation must be appropriate for the algorithm being used.
reviewSteps: Verify that nonces, initialization vectors, and other single-use numbers are not used for more than one encryption key and data-element pair. The method of generation must be appropriate for the algorithm being used.

asvs.name: V11.3.5 Encryption Algorithms
asvs.description: Verify that any combination of an encryption algorithm and a MAC algorithm is operating in encrypt-then-MAC mode.
reviewSteps: Verify that any combination of an encryption algorithm and a MAC algorithm is operating in encrypt-then-MAC mode.

asvs.name: V11.4.1 Hashing and Hash-based Functions
asvs.description: Verify that only approved hash functions are used for general cryptographic use cases, including digital signatures, HMAC, KDF, and random bit generation. Disallowed hash functions, such as MD5, must not be used for any cryptographic purpose.
reviewSteps: Verify that only approved hash functions are used for general cryptographic use cases, including digital signatures, HMAC, KDF, and random bit generation. Disallowed hash functions, such as MD5, must not be used for any cryptographic purpose.

asvs.name: V11.4.2 Hashing and Hash-based Functions
asvs.description: Verify that passwords are stored using an approved, computationally intensive, key derivation function (also known as a "password hashing function"), with parameter settings configured based on current guidance. The settings should balance security and performance to make brute-force attacks sufficiently challenging for the required level of security.
reviewSteps: Verify that passwords are stored using an approved, computationally intensive, key derivation function (also known as a "password hashing function"), with parameter settings configured based on current guidance. The settings should balance security and performance to make brute-force attacks sufficiently challenging for the required level of security.

asvs.name: V11.4.3 Hashing and Hash-based Functions
asvs.description: Verify that hash functions used in digital signatures, as part of data authentication or data integrity are collision resistant and have appropriate bit-lengths. If collision resistance is required, the output length must be at least 256 bits. If only resistance to second pre-image attacks is required, the output length must be at least 128 bits.
reviewSteps: Verify that hash functions used in digital signatures, as part of data authentication or data integrity are collision resistant and have appropriate bit-lengths. If collision resistance is required, the output length must be at least 256 bits. If only resistance to second pre-image attacks is required, the output length must be at least 128 bits.

asvs.name: V11.4.4 Hashing and Hash-based Functions
asvs.description: Verify that the application uses approved key derivation functions with key stretching parameters when deriving secret keys from passwords. The parameters in use must balance security and performance to prevent brute-force attacks from compromising the resulting cryptographic key.
reviewSteps: Verify that the application uses approved key derivation functions with key stretching parameters when deriving secret keys from passwords. The parameters in use must balance security and performance to prevent brute-force attacks from compromising the resulting cryptographic key.

asvs.name: V11.5.1 Random Values
asvs.description: Verify that all random numbers and strings which are intended to be non-guessable must be generated using a cryptographically secure pseudo-random number generator (CSPRNG) and have at least 128 bits of entropy. Note that UUIDs do not respect this condition.
reviewSteps: Verify that all random numbers and strings which are intended to be non-guessable must be generated using a cryptographically secure pseudo-random number generator (CSPRNG) and have at least 128 bits of entropy. Note that UUIDs do not respect this condition.

asvs.name: V11.5.2 Random Values
asvs.description: Verify that the random number generation mechanism in use is designed to work securely, even under heavy demand.
reviewSteps: Verify that the random number generation mechanism in use is designed to work securely, even under heavy demand.

asvs.name: V11.6.1 Public Key Cryptography
asvs.description: Verify that only approved cryptographic algorithms and modes of operation are used for key generation and seeding, and digital signature generation and verification. Key generation algorithms must not generate insecure keys vulnerable to known attacks, for example, RSA keys which are vulnerable to Fermat factorization.
reviewSteps: Verify that only approved cryptographic algorithms and modes of operation are used for key generation and seeding, and digital signature generation and verification. Key generation algorithms must not generate insecure keys vulnerable to known attacks, for example, RSA keys which are vulnerable to Fermat factorization.

asvs.name: V11.6.2 Public Key Cryptography
asvs.description: Verify that approved cryptographic algorithms are used for key exchange (such as Diffie-Hellman) with a focus on ensuring that key exchange mechanisms use secure parameters. This will prevent attacks on the key establishment process which could lead to adversary-in-the-middle attacks or cryptographic breaks.
reviewSteps: Verify that approved cryptographic algorithms are used for key exchange (such as Diffie-Hellman) with a focus on ensuring that key exchange mechanisms use secure parameters. This will prevent attacks on the key establishment process which could lead to adversary-in-the-middle attacks or cryptographic breaks.

asvs.name: V11.7.1 In-Use Data Cryptography
asvs.description: Verify that full memory encryption is in use that protects sensitive data while it is in use, preventing access by unauthorized users or processes.
reviewSteps: Verify that full memory encryption is in use that protects sensitive data while it is in use, preventing access by unauthorized users or processes.

asvs.name: V11.7.2 In-Use Data Cryptography
asvs.description: Verify that data minimization ensures the minimal amount of data is exposed during processing, and ensure that data is encrypted immediately after use or as soon as feasible.
reviewSteps: Verify that data minimization ensures the minimal amount of data is exposed during processing, and ensure that data is encrypted immediately after use or as soon as feasible.

asvs.name: V12.1.1 General TLS Security Guidance
asvs.description: Verify that only the latest recommended versions of the TLS protocol are enabled, such as TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3. The latest version of the TLS protocol must be the preferred option.
reviewSteps: Verify that only the latest recommended versions of the TLS protocol are enabled, such as TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3. The latest version of the TLS protocol must be the preferred option.

asvs.name: V12.1.2 General TLS Security Guidance
asvs.description: Verify that only recommended cipher suites are enabled, with the strongest cipher suites set as preferred. L3 applications must only support cipher suites which provide forward secrecy.
reviewSteps: Verify that only recommended cipher suites are enabled, with the strongest cipher suites set as preferred. L3 applications must only support cipher suites which provide forward secrecy.

asvs.name: V12.1.3 General TLS Security Guidance
asvs.description: Verify that the application validates that mTLS client certificates are trusted before using the certificate identity for authentication or authorization.
reviewSteps: Verify that the application validates that mTLS client certificates are trusted before using the certificate identity for authentication or authorization.

asvs.name: V12.1.4 General TLS Security Guidance
asvs.description: Verify that proper certification revocation, such as Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) Stapling, is enabled and configured.
reviewSteps: Verify that proper certification revocation, such as Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) Stapling, is enabled and configured.

asvs.name: V12.1.5 General TLS Security Guidance
asvs.description: Verify that Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) is enabled in the application's TLS settings to prevent exposure of sensitive metadata, such as the Server Name Indication (SNI), during TLS handshake processes.
reviewSteps: Verify that Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) is enabled in the application's TLS settings to prevent exposure of sensitive metadata, such as the Server Name Indication (SNI), during TLS handshake processes.

asvs.name: V12.2.1 HTTPS Communication with External Facing Services
asvs.description: Verify that TLS is used for all connectivity between a client and external facing, HTTP-based services, and does not fall back to insecure or unencrypted communications.
reviewSteps: Verify that TLS is used for all connectivity between a client and external facing, HTTP-based services, and does not fall back to insecure or unencrypted communications.

asvs.name: V12.2.2 HTTPS Communication with External Facing Services
asvs.description: Verify that external facing services use publicly trusted TLS certificates.
reviewSteps: Verify that external facing services use publicly trusted TLS certificates.

asvs.name: V12.3.1 General Service to Service Communication Security
asvs.description: Verify that an encrypted protocol such as TLS is used for all inbound and outbound connections to and from the application, including monitoring systems, management tools, remote access and SSH, middleware, databases, mainframes, partner systems, or external APIs. The server must not fall back to insecure or unencrypted protocols.
reviewSteps: Verify that an encrypted protocol such as TLS is used for all inbound and outbound connections to and from the application, including monitoring systems, management tools, remote access and SSH, middleware, databases, mainframes, partner systems, or external APIs. The server must not fall back to insecure or unencrypted protocols.

asvs.name: V12.3.2 General Service to Service Communication Security
asvs.description: Verify that TLS clients validate certificates received before communicating with a TLS server.
reviewSteps: Verify that TLS clients validate certificates received before communicating with a TLS server.

asvs.name: V12.3.3 General Service to Service Communication Security
asvs.description: Verify that TLS or another appropriate transport encryption mechanism used for all connectivity between internal, HTTP-based services within the application, and does not fall back to insecure or unencrypted communications.
reviewSteps: Verify that TLS or another appropriate transport encryption mechanism used for all connectivity between internal, HTTP-based services within the application, and does not fall back to insecure or unencrypted communications.

asvs.name: V12.3.4 General Service to Service Communication Security
asvs.description: Verify that TLS connections between internal services use trusted certificates. Where internally generated or self-signed certificates are used, the consuming service must be configured to only trust specific internal CAs and specific self-signed certificates.
reviewSteps: Verify that TLS connections between internal services use trusted certificates. Where internally generated or self-signed certificates are used, the consuming service must be configured to only trust specific internal CAs and specific self-signed certificates.

asvs.name: V12.3.5 General Service to Service Communication Security
asvs.description: Verify that services communicating internally within a system (intra-service communications) use strong authentication to ensure that each endpoint is verified. Strong authentication methods, such as TLS client authentication, must be employed to ensure identity, using public-key infrastructure and mechanisms that are resistant to replay attacks. For microservice architectures, consider using a service mesh to simplify certificate management and enhance security.
reviewSteps: Verify that services communicating internally within a system (intra-service communications) use strong authentication to ensure that each endpoint is verified. Strong authentication methods, such as TLS client authentication, must be employed to ensure identity, using public-key infrastructure and mechanisms that are resistant to replay attacks. For microservice architectures, consider using a service mesh to simplify certificate management and enhance security.

asvs.name: V13.1.1 Configuration Documentation
asvs.description: Verify that all communication needs for the application are documented. This must include external services which the application relies upon and cases where an end user might be able to provide an external location to which the application will then connect.
reviewSteps: Verify that all communication needs for the application are documented. This must include external services which the application relies upon and cases where an end user might be able to provide an external location to which the application will then connect.

asvs.name: V13.1.2 Configuration Documentation
asvs.description: Verify that for each service the application uses, the documentation defines the maximum number of concurrent connections (e.g., connection pool limits) and how the application behaves when that limit is reached, including any fallback or recovery mechanisms, to prevent denial of service conditions.
reviewSteps: Verify that for each service the application uses, the documentation defines the maximum number of concurrent connections (e.g., connection pool limits) and how the application behaves when that limit is reached, including any fallback or recovery mechanisms, to prevent denial of service conditions.

asvs.name: V13.1.3 Configuration Documentation
asvs.description: Verify that the application documentation defines resource‑management strategies for every external system or service it uses (e.g., databases, file handles, threads, HTTP connections). This should include resource‑release procedures, timeout settings, failure handling, and where retry logic is implemented, specifying retry limits, delays, and back‑off algorithms. For synchronous HTTP request–response operations it should mandate short timeouts and either disable retries or strictly limit retries to prevent cascading delays and resource exhaustion.
reviewSteps: Verify that the application documentation defines resource‑management strategies for every external system or service it uses (e.g., databases, file handles, threads, HTTP connections). This should include resource‑release procedures, timeout settings, failure handling, and where retry logic is implemented, specifying retry limits, delays, and back‑off algorithms. For synchronous HTTP request–response operations it should mandate short timeouts and either disable retries or strictly limit retries to prevent cascading delays and resource exhaustion.

asvs.name: V13.1.4 Configuration Documentation
asvs.description: Verify that the application's documentation defines the secrets that are critical for the security of the application and a schedule for rotating them, based on the organization's threat model and business requirements.
reviewSteps: Verify that the application's documentation defines the secrets that are critical for the security of the application and a schedule for rotating them, based on the organization's threat model and business requirements.

asvs.name: V13.2.1 Backend Communication Configuration
asvs.description: Verify that communications between backend application components that don't support the application's standard user session mechanism, including APIs, middleware, and data layers, are authenticated. Authentication must use individual service accounts, short-term tokens, or certificate-based authentication and not unchanging credentials such as passwords, API keys, or shared accounts with privileged access.
reviewSteps: Verify that communications between backend application components that don't support the application's standard user session mechanism, including APIs, middleware, and data layers, are authenticated. Authentication must use individual service accounts, short-term tokens, or certificate-based authentication and not unchanging credentials such as passwords, API keys, or shared accounts with privileged access.

asvs.name: V13.2.2 Backend Communication Configuration
asvs.description: Verify that communications between backend application components, including local or operating system services, APIs, middleware, and data layers, are performed with accounts assigned the least necessary privileges.
reviewSteps: Verify that communications between backend application components, including local or operating system services, APIs, middleware, and data layers, are performed with accounts assigned the least necessary privileges.

asvs.name: V13.2.3 Backend Communication Configuration
asvs.description: Verify that if a credential has to be used for service authentication, the credential being used by the consumer is not a default credential (e.g., root/root or admin/admin).
reviewSteps: Verify that if a credential has to be used for service authentication, the credential being used by the consumer is not a default credential (e.g., root/root or admin/admin).

asvs.name: V13.2.4 Backend Communication Configuration
asvs.description: Verify that an allowlist is used to define the external resources or systems with which the application is permitted to communicate (e.g., for outbound requests, data loads, or file access). This allowlist can be implemented at the application layer, web server, firewall, or a combination of different layers.
reviewSteps: Verify that an allowlist is used to define the external resources or systems with which the application is permitted to communicate (e.g., for outbound requests, data loads, or file access). This allowlist can be implemented at the application layer, web server, firewall, or a combination of different layers.

asvs.name: V13.2.5 Backend Communication Configuration
asvs.description: Verify that the web or application server is configured with an allowlist of resources or systems to which the server can send requests or load data or files from.
reviewSteps: Verify that the web or application server is configured with an allowlist of resources or systems to which the server can send requests or load data or files from.

asvs.name: V13.2.6 Backend Communication Configuration
asvs.description: Verify that where the application connects to separate services, it follows the documented configuration for each connection, such as maximum parallel connections, behavior when maximum allowed connections is reached, connection timeouts, and retry strategies.
reviewSteps: Verify that where the application connects to separate services, it follows the documented configuration for each connection, such as maximum parallel connections, behavior when maximum allowed connections is reached, connection timeouts, and retry strategies.

asvs.name: V13.3.1 Secret Management
asvs.description: Verify that a secrets management solution, such as a key vault, is used to securely create, store, control access to, and destroy backend secrets. These could include passwords, key material, integrations with databases and third-party systems, keys and seeds for time-based tokens, other internal secrets, and API keys. Secrets must not be included in application source code or included in build artifacts. For an L3 application, this must involve a hardware-backed solution such as an HSM.
reviewSteps: Verify that a secrets management solution, such as a key vault, is used to securely create, store, control access to, and destroy backend secrets. These could include passwords, key material, integrations with databases and third-party systems, keys and seeds for time-based tokens, other internal secrets, and API keys. Secrets must not be included in application source code or included in build artifacts. For an L3 application, this must involve a hardware-backed solution such as an HSM.

asvs.name: V13.3.2 Secret Management
asvs.description: Verify that access to secret assets adheres to the principle of least privilege.
reviewSteps: Verify that access to secret assets adheres to the principle of least privilege.

asvs.name: V13.3.3 Secret Management
asvs.description: Verify that all cryptographic operations are performed using an isolated security module (such as a vault or hardware security module) to securely manage and protect key material from exposure outside of the security module.
reviewSteps: Verify that all cryptographic operations are performed using an isolated security module (such as a vault or hardware security module) to securely manage and protect key material from exposure outside of the security module.

asvs.name: V13.3.4 Secret Management
asvs.description: Verify that secrets are configured to expire and be rotated based on the application's documentation.
reviewSteps: Verify that secrets are configured to expire and be rotated based on the application's documentation.

asvs.name: V13.4.1 Unintended Information Leakage
asvs.description: Verify that the application is deployed either without any source control metadata, including the .git or .svn folders, or in a way that these folders are inaccessible both externally and to the application itself.
reviewSteps: Verify that the application is deployed either without any source control metadata, including the .git or .svn folders, or in a way that these folders are inaccessible both externally and to the application itself.

asvs.name: V13.4.2 Unintended Information Leakage
asvs.description: Verify that debug modes are disabled for all components in production environments to prevent exposure of debugging features and information leakage.
reviewSteps: Verify that debug modes are disabled for all components in production environments to prevent exposure of debugging features and information leakage.

asvs.name: V13.4.3 Unintended Information Leakage
asvs.description: Verify that web servers do not expose directory listings to clients unless explicitly intended.
reviewSteps: Verify that web servers do not expose directory listings to clients unless explicitly intended.

asvs.name: V13.4.4 Unintended Information Leakage
asvs.description: Verify that using the HTTP TRACE method is not supported in production environments, to avoid potential information leakage.
reviewSteps: Verify that using the HTTP TRACE method is not supported in production environments, to avoid potential information leakage.

asvs.name: V13.4.5 Unintended Information Leakage
asvs.description: Verify that documentation (such as for internal APIs) and monitoring endpoints are not exposed unless explicitly intended.
reviewSteps: Verify that documentation (such as for internal APIs) and monitoring endpoints are not exposed unless explicitly intended.

asvs.name: V13.4.6 Unintended Information Leakage
asvs.description: Verify that the application does not expose detailed version information of backend components.
reviewSteps: Verify that the application does not expose detailed version information of backend components.

asvs.name: V13.4.7 Unintended Information Leakage
asvs.description: Verify that the web tier is configured to only serve files with specific file extensions to prevent unintentional information, configuration, and source code leakage.
reviewSteps: Verify that the web tier is configured to only serve files with specific file extensions to prevent unintentional information, configuration, and source code leakage.

asvs.name: V14.1.1 Data Protection Documentation
asvs.description: Verify that all sensitive data created and processed by the application has been identified and classified into protection levels. This includes data that is only encoded and therefore easily decoded, such as Base64 strings or the plaintext payload inside a JWT. Protection levels need to take into account any data protection and privacy regulations and standards which the application is required to comply with.
reviewSteps: Verify that all sensitive data created and processed by the application has been identified and classified into protection levels. This includes data that is only encoded and therefore easily decoded, such as Base64 strings or the plaintext payload inside a JWT. Protection levels need to take into account any data protection and privacy regulations and standards which the application is required to comply with.

asvs.name: V14.1.2 Data Protection Documentation
asvs.description: Verify that all sensitive data protection levels have a documented set of protection requirements. This must include (but not be limited to) requirements related to general encryption, integrity verification, retention, how the data is to be logged, access controls around sensitive data in logs, database-level encryption, privacy and privacy-enhancing technologies to be used, and other confidentiality requirements.
reviewSteps: Verify that all sensitive data protection levels have a documented set of protection requirements. This must include (but not be limited to) requirements related to general encryption, integrity verification, retention, how the data is to be logged, access controls around sensitive data in logs, database-level encryption, privacy and privacy-enhancing technologies to be used, and other confidentiality requirements.

asvs.name: V14.2.1 General Data Protection
asvs.description: Verify that sensitive data is only sent to the server in the HTTP message body or header fields, and that the URL and query string do not contain sensitive information, such as an API key or session token.
reviewSteps: Verify that sensitive data is only sent to the server in the HTTP message body or header fields, and that the URL and query string do not contain sensitive information, such as an API key or session token.

asvs.name: V14.2.2 General Data Protection
asvs.description: Verify that the application prevents sensitive data from being cached in server components, such as load balancers and application caches, or ensures that the data is securely purged after use.
